alignment.note: ὅτι / ܕ- (prefixed to ܗܐ) / Quia — recitative conjunction introducing direct speech.
ἰδού / ܗܐ / ecce — the Syriac fuses the conjunction and the deictic particle into the single proclitic form ܕܗܐ, hence the shared index.

Greek and Latin express the first-person plural verb synthetically (ἀναβαίνομεν / ascendimus); Syriac uses the participle ܣܠܩܝܢ followed by the enclitic pronoun ܚܢܢ ('we'), an analytic construction typical of Syriac present-tense narration.

Greek requires the preposition εἰς plus the accusative toponym Ἱεροσόλυμα; Latin uses the bare accusative of place-to-which Jerosolymam without preposition; Syriac employs the proclitic directional ܠ- on ܐܘܪܫܠܡ — three distinct strategies for the same allative sense. The parenthetical transliteration token (5) is editorial and carries no semantic weight.

ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου / ܘܒܪܗ ܕܐܢܫܐ / Filius hominis — the Syriac carries the conjunction ܘ- ('and') proclitically on ܒܪܗ, matching Greek καί (idx 5) which has been grouped with the preceding allative phrase per the Syriac word-division.
παραδοθήσεται / ܡܫܬܠܡ / tradetur — future/present passive 'will be handed over,' Syriac Ethpaal participle of š-l-m.
τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν / ܠܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ / principibus sacerdotum — 'to the chief priests,' rendered as a construct/genitive phrase ('chiefs of the priests') in both Syriac and Latin.
καί / ܘ- / et — coordinating conjunction; the Syriac ܘ- is proclitic to ܠܣܦܪܐ.
τοῖς γραμματεῦσιν / ܠܣܦܪܐ / scribis — 'to the scribes'; Syriac fuses conjunction, dative ܠ-, and noun into ܘܠܣܦܪܐ.

The Clementine Vulgate adds 'et senioribus' ('and to the elders'), harmonising toward the parallel passion-prediction lists (cf. Mark 8:31; Matt 16:21), where chief priests, scribes, and elders appear together. Neither the Greek NA28 nor the Peshitta transmit 'elders' at this point.
καί / ܘ- (proclitic on ܢܚܝܒܘܢܝܗܝ) / et — coordinating conjunction.

Greek κατακρινοῦσιν αὐτόν and Latin damnabunt eum express verb plus separate accusative object pronoun; Syriac ܢܚܝܒܘܢܝܗܝ incorporates the third-person object suffix directly onto the Pael verb of d-kh-b/ḥ-y-b ('they will condemn him'), a synthetic pronominal-object construction.
θανάτῳ / ܠܡܘܬܐ / morte — dative/ablative of penalty 'to death,' Syriac using directional ܠ-.

As with the previous verb, Greek παραδώσουσιν αὐτόν and Latin tradent eum use a separate object pronoun, whereas Syriac ܢܫܠܡܘܢܝܗܝ encloses the third-person masculine suffix on the verb of š-l-m ('and they will hand him over').
τοῖς ἔθνεσιν / ܠܥܡܡܐ / gentibus — 'to the Gentiles/nations,' Syriac plural of e-m-m with directional ܠ-.
The Clementine Vulgate closes the verse with a colon, marking the syntactic continuation into the following clause (v. 34). Greek and Syriac editions carry no equivalent terminal punctuation here.
